10. PWs 3 and 4 specifically stated about the gharoa bantannama between the predecessors of the plaintiffs and the defendants and about the possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land on such gharoa bantannama. It further appears that the trial Court considered the testimony of PW 1 (plaintiff No. 3 Was examined as PW1 ) in his cross examination only and found fault with his testimony on the ground that he could not say the total area of the land though he asserted that they were in possession of the half of the suit plot being No.185. The trial Court disbelieved PWs 2 and 3 on the ground that they could not tell the chauhaddi of suit plot No.214 though both of them specifically stated about the possession of the plaintiffs therein. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence of the DWs (2DWs were examined, DW No.1 being defendant No. 1) came to the finding that from the evidence of the DWs, no proof was found how much land of the suit land the defendants possess and how they possess (in the judgment, in Bangla, it has been written as "বিবাদীপক্ষের স্বাক্ষীদের বক্তব্য হইতে ও নালিশী সম্পত্তি কতটুকু কিভাবে ব��বাদীপক্ষ দখল করেন ইহার কোন প্রমাণ পাওয়া যায় না।") However, the trial Court noted that DWI in his examination-in-chief stated that the plaintiffs possess 1/3rd  of the suit land and they possess 2/3rd thereof and DW2 also stated that the defendants possess the major portion of the suit land and the plaintiffs possess less portion thereof, In coming to the facium of exclusive possession, the trial Court did not at all consider the S.A. khatians prepared in the name of the plaintiffs in respect of the suit land and the payment of rents by them for the same. The Appellate Court in spite of being the last Court of fact, did not consider the evidence at all either documentary or oral; it simply dittoed the finding of the trial Court in a slip shod manner. 

 "In the present case, it appears that the witnesses of the plaintiffs as well as that of defendants clearly deposed that there was an amicable partition 22/25 years back and the plaintiffs and defendants are possessing the land according to their shares, and without considering the evidence of the witnesses of both the parties, the Courts below took an erroneous view that there was no partition and as such the plaintiffs were not in possession of the suit land, It appears from the record that the plaintiffs mutated their names in the record of right and by virtue of that, they paid rents by exhibit-5 series and mutation in S.A. Khatian No. 31/7, 31/8 show their exclusive title and possession. In the present case the defendants' witnesses did not deny the partition as well as possession of the plaintiffs on the suit land. Although the trial Court found a primafacie case in favour of the plaintiffs, which, was mentioned in its judgment, dismissed the suit. The Court of appeal below affirmed it in a slip shod manner. The rent receipts, exhibit-5 series, though not document of title, are important items of evidence of possession and may be used as collateral evidence of title since possession generally follows title. Central point for consideration of the Court in a suit for permanent injunction is the question of possession, which requires to be decided mainly on oral evidence adduced by the contending parties and documentary evidence usually plays a secondary role. The trial Court ignored the evidence of the witnesses examined by the contending parties while passing the judgment and the Court of appeal below committed the same mistake by failing to discuss and consider the material evidence adduced by the contending parties. The witnesses of both the parties categorically deposed that there was a partition and the parties were possessing the land as per their shares," 

 12. The plaintiffs prayed for a decree for permanent injunction in respect of the suit land measuring an area of 2.46 acres land in 6(six) plots being Nos. 180, 214, 185, 130, 235 and 258 as described in schedule 'Ga' to the plaint. Area of the land in each of the plots has been specifically identified by chauhaddis. Before the trial Court, the attested certified copies of the SA. khatians were filed, but were not marked as exhibits. However, Mr. Bhuiyan could not dispute the correctness of the attested copies of the khatians, The khatians show that the names of the plaintiffs were recorded separately in respect of the suit land, The vital document proved and exhibited were the rent receipts, exhibit-5 series. These exhibits show that the plain-tiffs have been paying rents in respect of the suit land, In each of the rent receipt of exhihit-5 series, all the suit plots have been mentioned and the area mentioned is 2.46, i.e. the suit land. These facts clearly substantiate the ease of the plaintiffs that there was an amicable partition amongst the co-sharers and the suit land fell in the saham of the plaintiffs and they have been in possession thereof Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan found it difficult to dislodge the legal impact of S.A. Khatian and the payment of rents separately by the plaintiffs in respect of the suit land visa-vis the oral evidence of the PWs as was found by the High Court Division. 

 15. The trial Court also misread the evidence of the PWs as well as the DWs on the question of amicable partition in coming to the finding that the plaintiffs failed to prove their exclusive possession in the suit land, The trial Court did not also consider the S.A. Khatians recorded in the name of the plaintiffs and the rent receipts, exhibit-'5' series in that respect. Therefore, we do not see any wrong with the High Court Division in considering the evidence on record and give its finding on the question of exclusive possession of the suit land, particularly, in view of the fact that both the Courts below failed to consider the S.A. khatians and the rent receipts. Since the entire record was before the High Court Division, it had every right to go through the record and see whether the Courts below were correct in dismissing the suit on the ground that the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the suit land, From the findings of the High Court Division, it appears to us that it, in fact, considered the evidence, both oral and documentary, which the Courts failed to consider as well as misread. The instant case was a clear case of misreading and non-consideration of the material evidence by the Courts below. Therefore, it cannot be said that the High Court Division "re-appreciated" the evidence or in other words, re-assessed the evidence.
